paras: The attempted lynching of E. J. Wright took place at Pocatello, Idaho, on December 22, 1888, when a mob of railroad switchmen and brakemen surrounded the depot where officers held Wright after he shot a brakeman, L. F. Durfee. Wright was first reported dying of a neck wound, but a week later he was recovering in the Blackfoot jail after a coroner's jury exonerated him.

According to the Salt Lake Herald, Durfee, a passenger brakeman on the Oregon Short Line, fought at the Pacific Hotel with Constable Neilson, who called on Wright, known as "Buck," for help. Wright drew a gun in that row but was stopped.

About 2:30 p.m. Wright met Durfee in Dr. Bean's drug store and, in the Herald's words, "without a word" shot him twice in the face, killing him. Wright surrendered, escaped about 5:30 p.m., and was brought down by a bullet in the neck; the dispatch does not say who fired, though the headline blamed "the Mob." Officers took him to the depot, where railroad men gathered "intent on lynching him," and held them off with drawn revolvers until Sheriff Taylor arrived by extra train with a posse.

By December 29 Wright was in jail at Blackfoot, "improving slowly for one so dangerously wounded." The inquest cleared him "from all blame," though a preliminary hearing was still to come, and no report of it was found. Durfee was buried in the Odd Fellows' Cemetery at Blackfoot.

The Salt Lake Herald ran the story on December 23 under the headlines "A Tragedy in Idaho" and "An Attempt to Lynch Wright," reporting Wright "fatally shot." The Idaho News at Blackfoot, headlining "The Pocatello Murder Case," withheld "all comments" until the case was settled. In Nevada the Lyon County Times gave it two sentences, calling Durfee "murdered" by Wright, "a butcher," and omitting the mob. No paper mentioned either man's race.

The Herald and the Nevada brief called Wright fatally wounded; the Blackfoot paper, a week later, said he was recovering. The Nevada item also dated the shooting "last Sunday" and put the wound in the head, not the neck.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of E. J. Wright
bases: After a fatal shooting, a crowd of railroad switchmen and brakemen surrounded the depot where officers held the wounded prisoner, reported as 'intent on lynching him' (A2); he was not taken and survived (A3).

A mob of railroad men besieged the depot to lynch Wright for killing Durfee (A2), but officers held it off and a week later Wright was reported alive and recovering in the Blackfoot jail (A3), so no one was killed by the mob; this was an attempted lynching.

Three reports agree that Wright shot Durfee and was himself badly wounded the same day (A2, A3, A4), and the Idaho News confirms that 'excitement ran high' and the sheriff came to prevent 'further bloodshed' (A3), though the explicit mob siege and lynching intent appear only in the Salt Lake Herald dispatches (A2).

accounts.label: Pocatello special dispatches
accounts.gist: Wright shot Durfee without a word after an earlier row, surrendered, escaped, and was shot in the neck by pursuers; a mob of railroad men surrounded the depot to lynch him while officers held them off; he was said to be dying.

accounts.label: Blackfoot county-seat paper
accounts.gist: The inquest exonerated Wright; he was in jail at Blackfoot improving from his wounds, awaiting a hearing, and the sheriff had rushed to Pocatello to prevent further bloodshed.

accounts.label: Coast news brief
accounts.gist: Wright, a butcher, murdered Durfee, escaped, and was captured within hours after being fatally shot in the head.

framing.detail: The Salt Lake Herald's stacked headlines ('A Tragedy in Idaho', 'An Attempt to Lynch Wright', 'Struck in the Neck by a Bullet From the Mob') reported the mob without approval or condemnation and called the whole affair 'a horrible tragedy'.
The Idaho News headlined 'The Pocatello Murder Case' but withheld 'an extended notice and all comments' until Wright's case was disposed of.
The Lyon County Times ran a two-sentence item calling Durfee 'murdered' and omitting the mob.

record_check.dossier: The mob's target was E. J. Wright, who survived; Durfee was killed by Wright in the shooting that set off the mob and is not a victim of the mob.
First dispatches said Wright was dying, but a week later he was in jail at Blackfoot improving slowly; the coroner's inquest exonerated him for the killing.
Wright had escaped and was shot during the pursuit; he was then back in officers' custody at the depot when the mob surrounded it.
No county named in the papers; Wright was jailed and Durfee buried at Blackfoot, from where the sheriff came.
Three white papers: Salt Lake Herald (Dec 23), Idaho News and Lyon County Times (both Dec 29).

info: Saturday, December 22, 1888; Durfee shot about 2:30 p.m., Wright escaped about 5:30 p.m.
Pocatello, Idaho: Dr. Bean's drug store (shooting of Durfee), then the railroad depot building (siege)

Mob target: E. J. ('Buck') Wright, shot in the neck while fleeing, reported dying (A2) but later improving in jail (A3). Durfee, a passenger brakeman, was killed by Wright in the shooting that preceded the mob.
Wright was accused of shooting and killing L. F. ('Lew') Durfee, a passenger brakeman on the Oregon Short Line, after a row at the Pacific Hotel involving Constable Neilson.
A 'howling mob of switchmen and brakemen'; the Herald's headline attributes Wright's neck wound to 'the Mob', while the dispatch says only that he was 'pursued and shot at frequently'.
Wright was not lynched; he was jailed at Blackfoot, recovering slowly, to have a preliminary hearing when well enough. No report of the hearing was found.
